description: Scott Spreitzer review, checked 7 Nov 2026: his Doc's Sports prices from $25 to $850, how the credit guarantee works, and what his runs leave out.
dek: A Las Vegas radio regular who has sold picks on Doc's Sports since April 2018. His packages run from $25 a day to $850 a season, losing packages earn more picks or store credit, and every record on his page is a run or total chosen by the seller.

short_answer: Scott Spreitzer is a real, named handicapper with a long media history, and he sells through Doc's Sports, a store that names its operator and publishes its prices. Doc's announced him as a new handicapper on 11 Apr 2018 and said his picks would be found exclusively on his Doc's page. In that narrow sense, buying his picks is a legitimate transaction.

Whether his picks make money is a different question, and nothing we could open answers it. His page shows more than 30 runs and totals, such as "150-97, 61%" since 26 Aug and "+15,360" in football, all chosen by the seller, with no full log of every pick, price and post time. A losing package earns more picks or store credit, not a refund.

Treat him as a seller with marketing records, not a proven winner. If you buy, buy short, record every pick yourself with the line and time you received it, and judge it after at least a few hundred picks.

guarantee: Every Spreitzer package is sold under the Doc's Sports guarantee, so the remedy is the same as for the rest of the roster. On packages of a week or longer, the page says that if the package "finishes at a loss, you can extend your service for free through our self-extend program." On one day packages the remedy is an account credit, usually $30, added the next morning around 11 a.m. Eastern.

Some daily packages count a small win as a failure: college basketball pays the credit unless the day makes at least $40, NHL unless it makes at least $35, and CFL unless it shows at least $30. We did not find cash refund terms on any page we opened. Losses on the bets themselves are never covered, and those are usually far larger than the package price.

claims_note: The NBA line explains the dollar figures: +21,405 becomes +107,025 for "nickel" ($500) players, so the figures assume $100 per unit. What they leave out is the losing runs around each streak and the prices taken. Several runs start on a date the seller picked, such as 26 Aug for the 150-97 run and 16 Oct 2021 for the CFL run, and a start date chosen after the fact can turn almost any history into a winning streak.

The page is not kept consistent with itself. On 7 Nov 2026 the same football run read "164-112" in one block and "164-111" in another, and the props run read "+10,545" in one place and "+10,575" in another. These are small gaps, but they show the numbers are marketing copy, not an audited log.

The contest claims are the most checkable kind of claim, because casinos run those contests. We searched for the Station Casinos and Westgate SuperContest results he cites and found no outside page confirming them today. That does not mean they are false; it means we could not verify them.
record: What a buyer can verify independently: nothing current. A third party contest result would count, and his bio cites two (a Station Casinos football contest record and a Westgate SuperContest top 20 finish), but we found no casino or news page confirming either in our searches today. We found no court or regulator record involving him.

What Spreitzer and Doc's publish: runs and totals by sport, chosen by the seller, on his Doc's page. We found no full, time stamped log of every paid pick with the line, the odds and the release time on any page we could open without paying. His free picks on Doc's are public one at a time, but we found no complete graded record of them either.

our_data.text: Watchdog grades picks captured from public posts before the game starts. In this edition no Scott Spreitzer pick account is matched to a Watchdog graded record, so we make no claim about how his picks perform.
our_data.context: For scale: his page advertises a 61% overall run, and Doc's own FAQ sets a goal of 60% winners. On the Watchdog board on 7 Nov 2026, {{over60}} of {{established}} established accounts (100 or more graded picks) were at 60% or better, and the median established account won {{median_win}}% of its picks. At standard -110 odds a bettor needs about 52.4% to break even.

customers_intro: Independent customer evidence on Scott Spreitzer is close to nonexistent. We found no review sample, no Reddit discussion and no forum thread about buying his picks; the one critical forum mention is a single 2011 post with no detail. Below is everything we found and how much weight it can carry.

customers.text: TheRX forum's service play rules list Scott Spreitzer among the services whose write ups members may not post. The rule says nothing about his results or customer experience; it only shows he is treated there as a paid seller.

A Better Business Bureau search for "Scott Spreitzer" returned no results. Trustpilot lists no reviews of docsports.com, the store he sells through. Web searches of TheRX, Covers and SBR found no thread with buyers describing his picks, and the betting subreddit posts we read never mention him.
For buyer reports on the store he sells through, see our Doc's Sports review. Those reports cover the Doc's roster in general, not Spreitzer in particular.

In a Sportsbook Review thread asking members to list the worst tout "scammers" they had seen, one member replied with just "Lang and spreitzer." He gave no reasons, no purchase details and no record, so this is an unsupported opinion, not evidence.
CapperTek, a handicapper review site, keeps a page for ScottWins.com under his name, but it shows no reviews or complaints.

conflicts: Spreitzer's free pick on his page on 7 Nov 2026 listed the line as "Offered at: BookMaker," an offshore sportsbook. The Doc's FAQ says: "We have a list of offshore sports book that we have complete confidence in." We did not see the terms of any deal between Doc's and BookMaker on the pages we opened. Pointing buyers to one named sportsbook is still a possible financial interest a buyer should keep in mind.
Offshore sportsbooks are not licensed by U.S. state regulators. Check the law where you live before you follow that advice.
strengths: A named person with a public media career, selling through a store with a named operator, a mailing address and a phone line.
Prices and guarantee terms are written out per package on his page, so a buyer can read the rules before paying.
Free picks and a "Free $60 Account" offer on Doc's let a reader see his style before buying.
concerns: No full public record. Every number on his page is a run or total chosen by the seller, often from a start date the seller picked.
The guarantee replaces a losing package with more picks or store credit. It never returns money and never covers betting losses.
Contest wins cited in his bio could not be confirmed in any outside source we opened.
His free picks name an offshore sportsbook, and the store's FAQ recommends offshore books.
checklist: Ask for every pick from the last 12 months with the line, the odds and the time it was sent. A list of hot runs is not a record.
Count units, not wins. A 60% record at heavy favorites can still lose money.
Read the guarantee for the words refund, credit and extension. Most "guarantees" in this business are credits.
Write down each pick yourself the moment you receive it, with the line you can actually get.
Give any handicapper a few hundred picks before you call them a winner. Short runs swing hard both ways.
faq: He is a real handicapper with a long Las Vegas radio and TV history, and he sells through Doc's Sports, which names its operator and publishes its prices. We could not verify that his picks win over time, because no full record of every pick is published.
How much does Scott Spreitzer cost?

On 7 Nov 2026 his Doc's Sports page sold one day packages for $25 to $30, weekly packages for $89 to $99, monthly packages for $279 to $325, and season packages from $495 (rest of football season) to $850 (NBA). Losing packages earn an extension or store credit, not a refund.
Does Scott Spreitzer have a verified record?
No current one that we could find. His page shows runs such as 150-97 since 26 Aug, chosen by the seller, and the contest results in his bio were not confirmed by any outside page we opened.

For the money you get his picks in up to eight sports with unit ratings, from a known name, with $25 to $30 daily entry points. What is unproven is whether those picks beat the roughly 52.4% needed at -110 over hundreds of plays, and a losing package only earns more of the same picks.
